column3: Names Allah as the Lord of the present people and their earliest fathers.
The rejection of messengers supplies only a broad contrary backdrop.
Directly repeats the Lordship of the audience and their earliest fathers.
Joins Allah's Lordship and sole divinity to creation of all things.
The preceding mercy from the Lord frames the same Lordship in the immediate passage.
Attributes death and subsequent life to one agent, in reverse sequence.
Directly pairs giving life and death with return to Him.
The adjacent verse defines the Lord as Lord of heavens, earth, and what lies between.
Voices the objection that even earliest fathers could be raised.
Affirms sole divinity, judgment, and return across the first and last life.
Shows an appeal to the ways of earlier people, contrasting inherited custom with the focus's shared Lord.
Identifies the Lord through Moses and Aaron but adds no life-death or ancestral scope.
Combines sole divinity, dominion of heaven and earth, and giving life and death.
Repeats the resurrection challenge concerning earliest fathers.
Places living and dying under Allah, Lord of the worlds.
Links Allah's Lordship, sole divinity, and universal creation.
Uses family relations in a legal context without connecting them to Lordship or life and death.
Attributes dominion and the giving of life and death to Allah alone.
Pairs giving life and death with decisive creative command.
Parental language occurs in a household narrative, not the focus's claim of shared Lordship.
Speaks of preserving a life ethically, not divine giving and taking of life.
Affirms Allah as the audience's Lord, sole deity, and sovereign creator.
Hope for forgiveness on judgment day is only indirectly related to death and life.
Adds death and burial as part of the divine ordering of human life.
Contrasts a ruler's claim over life and death with Abraham's confession of his Lord.
Addresses God as Lord and mentions first and last people, but in a provision narrative.
Describes a state of neither dying nor living, a contrary boundary to the focus's life-death authority.
Declares Allah Lord of heavens, earth, and all worlds.
A bare statement adds no interpretable link.
Portrays death's approach without attributing life and death or Lordship.
Parallels the Lordship of heavens, earth, and what lies between.
Earlier writings do not clarify the focus's ancestral or life-death claim.
Directly attributes causing death and giving life to Him.
Records the dismissal of resurrection promised to the speakers and their fathers.
Knowledge of earlier scripture offers no direct clarification of the focus.
A recompense from the Lord is only a general Lordship resonance.
Opponents reject new revelation by appeal to their earliest fathers.
Explicitly challenges following fathers who lack knowledge and guidance.
Labels recited signs as tales of the earliest people, a contrary inherited-tradition response.
Extends Lordship over the paired eastern and western horizons.
Mentions the destruction of earlier peoples, adding a historical dimension to divine power.
Asks who is the Lord of Moses and Aaron, without the focus's scope.
Explicitly says Allah gives life and causes death, against human counterfactual claims.
The following of later people after earlier ones gives only a temporal echo.
The nearby challenge to bring back forefathers directly develops the focus passage's death and ancestors.
Lists parental houses in a legal permission, with no theological connection.
Calls what the Lord sent tales of the earlier people, a contrary response to revelation.
Pairs living and dead as categories but does not attribute them to the Lord.
Directly affirms one God and no deity except Him.
Affirms reviving the dead and records their prior deeds and traces.
The paternal epithet does not clarify the focus.
Directly identifies Allah as the only deity and stresses His encompassing knowledge.
Earlier and later groups in punishment add only a remote temporal resonance.
Records the demand to bring back fathers as the stated challenge to clear signs.
Joins revelation from the Lord with the formula that there is no deity except Him.
Silence on that day adds no focused link.
Names Him Lord of Sirius but does not address life, death, or the generations.
Directly combines sole divinity with Lordship of the great throne.
Exclusive service to Allah is a general monotheistic resonance.
Refers to one's life in regret, without the focus's divine attribution.
Affirms Allah as the only deity, the Living and Sustaining.
Reception of recitation does not clarify the focus.
Praise to Allah, Lord of the worlds, offers a general Lordship echo.
Directly attributes life and death to Him and situates them within cosmic alternation.
The first house for people is not relevant to the focus claim.
Rejects signs as unheard of among earliest fathers, paralleling ancestral resistance.
Repeatedly testifies that there is no deity except Him, with divine witnessing and justice.
Inheritance of the garden does not clarify the focus.
Mentions mother and father only as family relations.
Directly affirms Allah as the sole deity and names His beautiful names.
Prayer for a father provides a limited ancestral resonance only.
Human ingratitude to his Lord does not explain the focus's claims.
Combines sole divinity with Allah's kingship and Lordship of the noble throne.
Earlier and later communities in punishment offer only a remote generational parallel.
Forgiveness by the speaker's Lord is not a direct aid to the focus.
Forbids calling another deity and affirms sole divinity, judgment, and return.
States the bodily-resurrection challenge after death, dust, and bones.
Earlier scriptures provide only a distant reference to the earliest.
Links Allah as sole deity with unique creation and provision from heaven and earth.
An earlier legal restriction and Torah challenge do not clarify the focus.
The Lord's awareness on that day is a general theological resonance.
Creation in wombs and sole divinity support divine creative authority, without the exact life-death pair.
Desire for a reminder from earlier people is not directly relevant.
Questions whether a message's absence among earliest fathers justifies rejecting it.
Traces human existence through death, life, death, renewed life, and return to Him.
Universal messenger call to worship Allah alone supports the focus's exclusive divinity.
Steadfast confession that our Lord is Allah has only a general Lordship link.
Affirms sole divinity and Lordship of the great throne amid turning away.
Noah's call to worship Allah alone provides a broad parallel for exclusive divinity.
A multitude from the earliest people has no direct interpretive role.
The exception for worshippers adds no focused link.
Fear your Lord before the Hour is a general eschatological Lordship resonance.
Patience and great fortune do not clarify the focus.
The Lord's action against Aad offers only a general authority resonance.
Ritual regulations do not clarify the focus claim.
Return to our Lord offers a general endpoint resonance.
Invokes one's Lord within debt regulation, not life, death, or ancestral Lordship.
Condemns equating others with the Lord of the worlds, reinforcing exclusive Lordship.
The messenger's warning role adds no focused link.
Fear of disobeying one's Lord on a great day is only a general authority resonance.
Commands the slain person be struck so Allah brings the dead to life.
States that Allah caused a multitude to die and then gave them life.
Affirms that there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living Sustainer.
Demonstrates resurrection after death through a man, his food, and his animal.
Shows Allah reviving dead birds at Abraham's request.
Attributes bringing living from dead and dead from living to Allah.
Declares that there is no deity except Allah.
Presents death as inescapable even in fortified towers.
Affirms Allah as the only deity and gathers people for the Day of Resurrection.
Rejects claims that compromise Allah's oneness.
Condemns taking the Messiah as God and directs worship to Allah as Lord.
Explicitly rejects saying that Allah is one of three gods.
Says Allah will raise the dead and they will return to Him.
Attributes bringing the living from the dead and the dead from the living to Allah.
Describes Allah giving life to one who was dead and granting light.
Names Allah as Lord of all things and denies another lord besides Him.
Links creation and command with Allah as Lord of the worlds.
Noah calls his people to worship Allah, with no deity besides Him.
Hud calls his people to worship Allah, with no deity besides Him.
Salih calls his people to worship Allah, with no deity besides Him.
Shuayb calls his people to worship Allah, with no deity besides Him.
Responding to Allah and the messenger is said to give life.
Contrasts taking religious lords with worshiping the one God.
Describes lives and possessions as belonging to Allah in exchange for the Garden.
Asks who brings living from dead and dead from living, then identifies Allah's governance.
Confesses that there is no deity except the One in whom Israel's children believe.
Calls the people to worship Allah, with no deity besides Him, as their originator.
Shuayb repeats the call to worship Allah alone.
Contrasts many separate lords with Allah, the One, the Prevailing.
Names Allah creator of all things and contrasts Him with claimed partners.
Affirms that He is Allah, with no deity except Him, and return is to Him.
Appeals to Allah as creator of heavens and earth against doubt in Him.
Proclaims one God so people may know that He is the One.
Directly says that We give life and cause death and are the inheritors.
Reveals that there is no deity except Allah and commands reverence for Him.
Forbids taking two gods and states that He is one God.
Uses revived earth after rain as a sign of Allah giving life.
States Allah creates, then causes death, within human life spans.
Affirms Allah's undivided dominion and rejects child, partner, and protector claims.
Confesses the Lord of heavens and earth and rejects calling another deity.
Says Allah shares His judgment with no one.
Pairs birth, death, and resurrection in a single human declaration.
Names the Lord of heavens, earth, and what lies between and asks whether any equal is known.
Argues that multiple gods in heaven and earth would have brought corruption.
States the recurring messenger command: no deity except Me, so worship Me.
Attributes creation of night and day, sun and moon, to Him.
Denies immortality for humans before the addressee.
States that every soul will taste death and will be tested.
Details human formation and resurrection after death.
Affirms that Allah gives life to the dead and has power over all things.
Affirms the Hour and Allah's raising of those in graves.
Directly says He gives life, causes death, and gives life again.
States that people will surely die after this.
States that people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection.
Rejects any god alongside Allah and any divine offspring.
Attributes dominion and creation of every thing in due measure to Allah.
Denies that claimed gods can create or control death, life, or resurrection.
Commands reliance on the Living One who does not die.
States that every soul will taste death and then return to Him.
Says Allah originates creation, repeats it, and people return to Him.
Attributes creation, provision, death, and life to Allah.
Uses revival of the earth as evidence that He gives life to the dead.
Attributes death to the angel assigned over people, followed by return to their Lord.
Uses dead earth revived for food as a sign of divine life-giving.
Sets out the objection about who revives decayed bones.
Answers that the One who created them first will revive them.
Affirms that the creator of heavens and earth can create their like.
Describes Allah taking souls at death and during sleep, then retaining or releasing them.
Names Allah as creator of all things and guardian over all things.
Describes death at the trumpet blast and renewed rising at the next blast.
Confesses two deaths and two lives, recognizing the resulting accountability.
Names Him the Living, with no deity except Him.
Uses earth's revival after rain as a sign that He revives the dead.
States that Allah gives life to the dead and has power over all things.
Uses life given to dead land as an analogy for being brought forth.
Says Allah gives life, causes death, and gathers people for the Day of Resurrection.
Argues that the creator of heavens and earth can give life to the dead.
Records the objection that return after death and dust is far-fetched.
Answers doubt about first creation with the prospect of new creation.
Directly says that We give life and cause death, and to Us is the destination.
Recalls that Allah created the hearers and challenges denial of that fact.
States that Allah has decreed death among people.
Links decreed death with replacing people and recreating them in an unknown form.
Invokes the first creation as grounds for reflection.
Attributes dominion, life, death, and power over all things to Allah.
States that He created death and life as a test.
Counters the assumption that scattered bones will not be gathered.
Asks whether the One who created human life is able to give life to the dead.
Calls the human being to consider from what he was created.
Affirms that Allah is able to return him.
